# RURQE (Rust Universal Relational Query Engine)

> Ergonomic, strictly type-safe SQL query builder, relational execution engine, and database-first codegen toolkit for Rust.

## Core Architectural Principles

- **Kysely Ergonomics (DX):** Queries read like idiomatic SQL. Named projection macros (`select!`, `cols!`, `dto!`) eliminate tuple indexing (`row.0`, `row.1`) without requiring manual struct boilerplate.
- **Strict Compile-Time Safety & Zero-Cost:** Zero-Sized Type (ZST) markers monomorphize into static SQL buffers and direct deserializers with zero runtime overhead.
- **Dialect & Version Capability Gating:** SQL features unsupported by a target database engine or version (`SupportsReturning`, `SupportsOnConflict`, `SupportsDistinctOn`) are gated via compile-time capability traits. Incompatible queries fail to compile.
- **Two-Tier SQL Correctness:** Relational scope, outer-join nullability, typestates, capability gates, `IN`-subquery arity/type congruence, aggregation provenance, and compound-statement ordering are enforced by the compiler on stable Rust. Rules that need negative assertions (unaliased duplicate relations) or clause alignment decided by a dynamic fluent chain (`DISTINCT ON` prefix, compound `ORDER BY` targets) are validated deterministically by the fallible `.build()`, which returns `Result<BuiltQuery, BuildError>` before any SQL leaves the process.
- **Typestate Protection:** Unfiltered `UPDATE` and `DELETE` operations fail at compile time unless explicitly scoped via `.where_(...)` or confirmed via `.allow_all()`.
- **Database-First Single Source of Truth:** Live database catalogs (PostgreSQL and SQLite) are introspected directly into strongly typed schemas, canonical `schema.lock` snapshots, and compile-time `SCHEMA_HASH` constants.
- **Flyway Lifecycle Integrity:** Migration runner supporting versioned (`V1__...`) and repeatable (`R__...`) scripts, standalone SHA-256 checksum audits, baseline onboarding, repair, and drift verification.
- **Stage + Migration Tail Lifecycle:** A declarative `rurqe/schema/` stage is the single source of truth for the target schema while the active `rurqe/migrations/` tail advances existing databases. A `rurqe/migrations/checkpoint.toml` marker records the pruned boundary and the stage hash, so folded history can be deleted without squashing, and `State(schema/) == State(Checkpoint + migrations/)` is verified in CI by the golden equation. One root-level `root` key of `rurqe.toml` (`rurqe` by default) relocates the whole artifact directory, and every path the document declares resolves against the directory holding the configuration file.

---

## Workspace Architecture & Feature Flags

- **`rurqe`**: Facade crate re-exporting the prelude, entrypoints, and runtime drivers.
  - Dialect preludes `rurqe::postgres::prelude::*` and `rurqe::sqlite::prelude::*` re-export the shared prelude with dialect-pinned, turbofish-free query entry points.
  - Feature `sqlite`: enables `rurqe-sqlite` and synchronous `rusqlite` integration.
  - Feature `postgres`: enables `rurqe-postgres` and synchronous `postgres` integration.
  - Feature `tokio-postgres`: enables asynchronous `tokio-postgres` client integration.
  - Feature `r2d2`: enables connection pooling for sync SQLite and sync PostgreSQL.
  - Feature `deadpool`: enables async connection pooling for `tokio-postgres`.
- **`rurqe-core`**: AST, expressions, schema markers (`Table`, `Column`, `ExprScope`), dialects, DML typestates, execution contracts (`QueryBackend`, `TransactionBackend`).
- **`rurqe-macros`**: Declarative and procedural macros (`table!`, `select!`, `cols!`, `dto!`, `sql!`, `raw_sql!`, `embed_migrations!`) and the `#[derive(SqlType)]` domain newtype derive. `embed_migrations!` scans a migrations directory at compile time and bakes every `*.sql` script of it into the binary through `include_str!`.
- **`rurqe-postgres`**: PostgreSQL dialect (`Postgres<V>`), version markers (`Pg14`, `Pg15`, `Pg16`), sync `PgConnection`, async `PgAsyncConnection`, and pool adapters. Behind its `migrate` feature it also carries the PostgreSQL half of the migration protocol — the history table, the advisory locks, the transactions, and the catalog introspection behind `SchemaCatalog` — together with the client backends that drive a connection an application already owns: `PgConnectionMigrationBackend` over the synchronous connection and `PgAsyncMigrationBackend` over the asynchronous clients and pools.
- **`rurqe-sqlite`**: SQLite dialect (`Sqlite<V>`), version bounds (`Sqlite3_0`, `Sqlite3_24`, `Sqlite3_35`), sync `SqliteConnection`, and `r2d2` pool. Behind its `migrate` feature it carries the same engine half for SQLite — `BEGIN IMMEDIATE` locking, savepoints, the migration backends, and catalog introspection — and the client backend `SqliteConnectionMigrationBackend`.
- **`rurqe-migrate`**: Flyway-compatible migration runner, in-memory SHA-256, `__rurqe_schema_history`, `EmbeddedMigrations`, `SchemaCatalog`, checkpoint markers (`Checkpoint`), cold start from the declarative stage (`DeclarativeStage`, `cold_start`), and the engine-neutral catalog vocabulary every driver shares — the `Raw*` metadata, the SQL-type mapping, and the catalog assembly.
- **`rurqe-project`**: The single copy of the `rurqe.toml` model — its strict `toml_edit` parser with positional diagnostics, `SchemaSelection`, `ConfigError`, the resolution of every declared path, and the discovery of the file itself — shared by the toolchain and the procedural macro crate.
- **`rurqe-cli`**: CLI toolchain (`cargo rurqe migrate`, `cargo rurqe codegen`, `cargo rurqe verify`, `cargo rurqe baseline`, plus the `cargo rurqe stage init|verify|commit|cleanup` and `cargo rurqe prune` lifecycle) with dual PostgreSQL and SQLite parity and golden-equation verification. It holds no engine protocol of its own: the backends and the introspection it drives come from the driver crates, so the protocol exists in one copy.
---

## Comprehensive Code Patterns

### 1. Schema Declaration

Schemas are declared with zero boilerplate using the `table!` macro:

```rust
use rurqe::prelude::*;

table!(
    /// The `users` table.
    User => "users" {
        UserId => "id": i64,
        UserName => "name": String,
        UserActive => "active": bool,
    }
);

table!(
    /// The `orders` table.
    Order => "orders" {
        OrderId => "id": i64,
        OrderUserId => "user_id": i64,
        OrderTotal => "total": f64,
    }
);
```

### 2. Relational Querying (Joins & Sound Nullability)

Columns from `LEFT JOIN` operations are lifted to `Option<T>` at compile time via `query.nullable::<Col>()`, preventing null dereference errors:

```rust
let query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .inner_join::<Order>(Expr::column::<OrderUserId>().eq(Expr::column::<UserId>()))
    .select((UserId, UserName, OrderTotal))
    .where_(Expr::column::<UserActive>().eq(true))
    .order_by_desc(UserId)
    .limit(10)
    .offset(20);

// Left join with automatic Option<T> lifting:
let left_query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .left_join::<Order>(Expr::column::<OrderUserId>().eq(Expr::column::<UserId>()))
    .select((UserId, UserName, left_query.nullable::<OrderTotal>()));
// Decoded row type: (i64, String, Option<f64>)
```

### 3. Named Projections (`cols!`, `select!`, `dto!`)

Eliminate anonymous tuple indexing (`row.0`) with ad-hoc records or named DTO structures:

```rust
// Ad-hoc record with cols!:
let query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .select(cols!(UserId, UserName as contact_name))
    .where_(Expr::column::<UserActive>().eq(true));

// Access fields directly by name:
// row.user_id, row.contact_name

// Reusable DTO structs with dto!:
dto! {
    #[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
    pub struct UserProfile {
        UserId,
        UserName as display_name,
    }
}

let query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .select(select!(UserProfile))
    .where_(Expr::column::<UserActive>().eq(true));
```

### 4. Aggregations, `GROUP BY`, and `HAVING`

```rust
// Group by first, then project the grouped columns, the aggregates, and the
// expressions built from them.
let query = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .group_by(OrderUserId)
    .select((OrderUserId, Expr::sum::<OrderTotal>(), Expr::count_all()))
    .having(Expr::sum::<OrderTotal>().gt(1000.0));
```

Aggregation provenance survives scalar functions: `coalesce`, `nullif`, `greatest`, and `least` accept every argument through `FunctionOperand` and fold the markers they contribute through `CombineAggr`, so a call stays an aggregate as soon as one argument aggregates — `coalesce(sum(orders.total), 0.0)` projects from a `GroupedQuery` without a cast or an explicit `.nullable()`:

```rust
let query = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .group_by(OrderUserId)
    .select((
        OrderUserId,
        coalesce(Expr::<f64>::sum::<OrderTotal>(), 0.0),
        nullif(Expr::<i64>::count_all(), 0i64),
        Expr::<i64>::case()
            .when(Expr::<i64>::count_all().gt(5i64), Expr::<i64>::count_all())
            .else_(0i64)
            .end(),
    ));
```

A per-row argument keeps the whole call per-row, so an ungrouped column hidden inside `coalesce` is still rejected by the compiler:

```text
group_by(users.id).select((users.id, coalesce(users.name, "anon"))) // rejected: `users.name` is neither grouped nor aggregated
```

### 5. Common Table Expressions (`WITH cte AS (...)`)

```rust
let active_orders = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .select((OrderId, OrderUserId))
    .where_(Expr::column::<OrderTotal>().gt(100.0));

let query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .with(cte_named("active_orders", active_orders))
    .select((UserId, UserName))
    .where_(Expr::column::<UserId>().gt(10i64));
```

### 6. Window Functions & Analytics (`OVER`)

```rust
let window = Window::partition_by(OrderUserId).order_by_desc(OrderTotal);

let query = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .select((
        OrderId,
        row_number().over(window.clone()),
        rank().over(window.clone()),
        dense_rank().over(window.clone()),
        lag(OrderTotal).offset(1).over(Window::order_by_asc(OrderId)),
        lead(OrderTotal).over(Window::order_by_asc(OrderId)),
    ));
```

### 7. Controlled Raw SQL Escape Hatch (`sql!`, `raw_sql!`)

Parameter binding prevents SQL injection and adapts automatically to dialect placeholders (`$1`, `$2` vs `?`):

```rust
// Positional placeholders `?` (escaped as `??`):
let custom_filter = sql!(
    bool,
    "EXTRACT(YEAR FROM created_at) = ? AND status = ?",
    2024i64,
    "active"
);

// Named format syntax `{}`:
let query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .select((UserId, sql!(<i64> "COUNT(*)")))
    .where_(raw_sql!("age >= {} AND active = {}", 18i64, true));
```

### 8. NULL Predicates & Conditional Expressions (`CASE WHEN`)

`IS NULL` / `IS NOT NULL` are type-safe methods on any expression, and `Expr::<T>::case()` builds a searched `CASE` expression whose branches must all produce `T`:

```rust
// IS NULL / IS NOT NULL predicates bind no parameters:
let query = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .select((OrderId,))
    .where_(Expr::column::<OrderTotal>().is_not_null());

// CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END producing String values:
let tier = Expr::<String>::case()
    .when(Expr::column::<OrderTotal>().gt(100.0), "large")
    .when(Expr::column::<OrderTotal>().gt(10.0), "medium")
    .else_("small")
    .end();

let query = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .select((OrderId, tier));
// Rendered: SELECT "id", CASE WHEN ("total" > $1) THEN $2 ... ELSE $5 END FROM "orders"
// Decoded row type: (i64, String)
```

`case()` requires at least one `when` branch; omitting `else_` leaves unmatched rows to the engine's `NULL`.

Branches fold the aggregation marker of their condition, their result, and the `ELSE` fallback the same way a scalar function folds its arguments, so a `CASE` written entirely over aggregates stays an aggregate and remains projectable from a `GroupedQuery`:

```rust
let tier = Expr::<i64>::case()
    .when(Expr::<i64>::count_all().gt(5i64), Expr::<i64>::count_all())
    .else_(0i64)
    .end();

let report = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .group_by(OrderUserId)
    .select((OrderUserId, tier));
```

A branch that reads a bare column makes the whole expression per-row, so the grouped query rejects it unless that column is grouped.

### 9. Subquery Predicates (`EXISTS`, `IN`)

`Expr::exists` / `Expr::not_exists` accept any `SelectQuery`, while `.in_subquery(...)` / `.not_in_subquery(...)` compare a column with the nested query. Nested statements render inline and continue the placeholder numbering of the enclosing query:

```rust
let big_spenders = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .select((OrderUserId,))
    .where_(Expr::column::<OrderTotal>().gt(100.0));

let query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .select((UserId,))
    .where_(Expr::column::<UserId>().in_subquery(big_spenders))
    .where_(Expr::not_exists(
        select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
            .select((OrderId,))
            .where_(Expr::column::<OrderTotal>().lt(5.0)),
    ));

// SELECT "id" FROM "users" WHERE (("id" IN (SELECT "user_id" FROM "orders" WHERE ("total" > $1)))
//   AND (NOT EXISTS (SELECT "id" FROM "orders" WHERE ("total" < $2))))
```

A `SelectQuery` also converts into a reusable subquery via `.into_subquery()`, `.exists()`, and `.not_exists()`.

### 10. Set Operations (`UNION`, `UNION ALL`, `INTERSECT`, `EXCEPT`)

Set operators combine two `SelectQuery<D, Tables, Output>` values. The dialect and the output row type are checked at compile time, so the combined statement stays decodable as `Output`.

A combined statement produces the columns of its first projection list, so the query moves into the `Compound` scope: its rows no longer belong to a table, and it can neither keep a row-level lock nor request one. Ordering a combined statement therefore goes through the result the combination produced instead of the tables its operands read — the table-qualified `.order_by*` family stops applying and two builders take its place:

- `order_by_output(_asc/_desc/_nulls_first/_nulls_last…)` names an output column;
- `order_by_index(_asc/_desc)` names a 1-based position of the projection list.

The first compound criterion moves the query into `TailClosed`, where another operand is rejected: SQL binds the trailing `ORDER BY` to the whole result, so `A UNION B ORDER BY ... UNION C` is invalid. A criterion written before a set operation belongs to the left operand and renders inside its parentheses, while `LIMIT` / `OFFSET` written after one apply to the combined rows.

`.build()` validates the assembled clause: `BuildError::CompoundOrderIndex` rejects a position outside the projection list and `BuildError::CompoundOrderColumn` rejects an output name the projection list does not produce.

```rust
let by_state = |active: bool| {
    select_from::<Postgres, User>()
        .select((UserId,))
        .where_(Expr::column::<UserActive>().eq(active))
};

let visible = by_state(true)
    .union_all(by_state(false))
    .order_by_output_asc(UserId)
    .limit(50)
    .build()
    .expect("valid query");
// SELECT "id" FROM "users" WHERE ("active" = $1)
// UNION ALL SELECT "id" FROM "users" WHERE ("active" = $2) ORDER BY "id" ASC LIMIT 50

// The same result ordered by the position of its single projected column:
let by_position = by_state(true).union(by_state(false)).order_by_index_desc(1);

// Deduplicating and filtering variants:
let deduped = by_state(true).union(by_state(false));
let both = by_state(true).intersect(by_state(false));
let only_active = by_state(true).except(by_state(false));
```

An operand can never be combined after the ordering of the combined rows, and a compound statement cannot be addressed by a constituent table's column:

```text
first.union(second).order_by_output_asc(UserId).union(third) // rejected: the tail is closed
first.union(second).order_by_asc(UserId)                     // rejected: no relation in scope
```

### 11. Type-Safe DML with Typestate Protection

Unfiltered `UPDATE` and `DELETE` queries will not compile without `.where_(...)` or `.allow_all()`.
`RETURNING` projections and `ON CONFLICT` targets may only reference columns of the mutated table, so a projection of an unrelated table fails to compile:

```rust
// INSERT with typed assignments and RETURNING
let (new_id,): (i64,) = insert_into::<Postgres, User>()
    .values((
        UserId::default_value(), // renders SQL DEFAULT keyword
        UserName::set("alice"),
        UserActive::set(true),
    ))
    .returning((UserId,))
    .fetch_one(&mut db)?;

// Bulk INSERT
insert_into::<Postgres, User>()
    .values_many(vec![
        (UserName::set("bob"), UserActive::set(true)),
        (UserName::set("carol"), UserActive::set(false)),
    ])
    .execute(&mut db)?;

// UPDATE with compile-time typestate guard
update::<Postgres, User>()
    .set(UserActive::set(false))
    .where_(Expr::column::<UserId>().eq(new_id))
    .execute(&mut db)?;

// Full-table update requires explicit allow_all()
update::<Postgres, User>()
    .set(UserActive::set(true))
    .allow_all()
    .execute(&mut db)?;

// DELETE with RETURNING
delete_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .where_(Expr::column::<UserId>().eq(new_id))
    .returning((UserName,))
    .fetch_optional(&mut db)?;

// UPSERT (ON CONFLICT) - gated by SupportsOnConflict capability
insert_into::<Postgres, User>()
    .values((UserId::set(1i64), UserName::set("root"), UserActive::set(true)))
    .on_conflict((UserId,))
    .do_update(UserName::set("root_updated"))
    .execute(&mut db)?;

// ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING
insert_into::<Postgres, User>()
    .values((UserId::set(1i64), UserName::set("root"), UserActive::set(true)))
    .on_conflict_do_nothing()
    .execute(&mut db)?;

// Database-side copy: INSERT INTO ... SELECT
insert_into::<Postgres, User>()
    .from_select(
        (UserId, UserName, UserActive),
        select_from::<Postgres, ArchivedUser>().select((ArchivedId, ArchivedName, ArchivedActive)),
    )
    .execute(&mut db)?;
```

### 12. Table Aliases & Self-Joins

`Aliased<T, A>` references table `T` under the alias `A`, while `AliasedCol<A, C>` addresses a column through that alias and keeps the column's `RustType`. Aliases keep self-joins unambiguous: `FROM` / `JOIN` render `"table" AS "alias"` and projections render `"alias"."column"`.

```rust
use rurqe::prelude::*;

table_alias! {
    /// The `manager` alias.
    ManagerAlias => "manager"
}

let built = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .inner_join::<Aliased<User, ManagerAlias>>(
        Expr::column::<UserManagerId>().eq(Expr::column::<AliasedCol<ManagerAlias, UserId>>()),
    )
    .select((
        UserId,
        UserName,
        AliasedCol::<ManagerAlias, UserId>::new(),
        AliasedCol::<ManagerAlias, UserName>::new(),
    ))
    .build();

// SELECT "id", "name", "manager"."id", "manager"."name" FROM "users"
//   INNER JOIN "users" AS "manager" ON ("manager_id" = "manager"."id")
```

Column markers are zero-sized values, so the same `AliasedCol<A, C>` marker is produced without turbofish noise through `UserId.alias::<A>()` or `A::col(UserId)`:

```rust
.select((
    UserId,
    UserName,
    UserId.alias::<ManagerAlias>(),
    ManagerAlias.col(UserName),
))

// SELECT "id", "name", "manager"."id", "manager"."name" FROM "users" ...
```

Columns of an aliased table introduced with `.left_join(...)` are lifted into `Option<T>` through `query.nullable::<AliasedCol<A, C>>()`.

### 13. LATERAL Joins

LATERAL joins require a dialect implementing `SupportsLateralJoin` (PostgreSQL). The inline subquery may reference columns of the tables to its left, expressing correlated per-row subqueries entirely on the database side.

```rust
let latest = select_from::<Postgres, Order>()
    .select((OrderTotal,))
    .where_(Expr::column::<OrderUserId>().eq(Expr::column::<UserId>()))
    .order_by_desc(OrderId)
    .limit(1);

let built = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .cross_join_lateral(latest.as_lateral::<RecentOrder>())
    .select((UserId, RecentTotal))
    .build();

// SELECT "id", "total" FROM "users" CROSS JOIN LATERAL
//   (SELECT "total" FROM "orders" WHERE ("user_id" = "id") ORDER BY "id" DESC LIMIT 1) AS "recent"
```

`left_join_lateral` renders `LEFT JOIN LATERAL ... ON true` and keeps outer rows a lateral subquery leaves unmatched, so its columns must be projected through `query.nullable::<...>()` to lift them into `Option<T>`.

### 14. Fluent Predicates (`LIKE`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`)

Pattern matching, range tests, and membership lists are first-class typed predicates available on columns and expressions. Every operand is bound as a parameter, and an incompatible value type fails to compile at the call site:

```rust
// Pattern matching: `like` is case-sensitive, `ilike` is case-insensitive.
let by_name = Expr::column::<UserName>()
    .like("A%")
    .or(Expr::column::<UserName>().ilike("%admin%"));

// Inclusive range and membership lists.
let ranged = Expr::column::<UserId>().between(10i64, 20i64);
let shortlisted = Expr::column::<UserId>().in_list(vec![1i64, 2i64, 3i64]);
let excluded = Expr::column::<UserName>().not_in_list(vec!["root", "admin"]);

let query = select_from::<Postgres, User>()
    .select((UserId, UserName))
    .where_(by_name)
    .where_(ranged)
    .where_(shortlisted)
    .where_(excluded);

// SELECT "id", "name" FROM "users"
//   WHERE (((("name" LIKE $1) OR ("name" ILIKE $2)) AND ("id" BETWEEN $3 AND $4))
//     AND ("id" IN ($5, $6, $7))) AND ("name" NOT IN ($8, $9))
```

`in_list` / `not_in_list` accept any iterator of compatible values and require at least one element; an empty list is a programming error caught by an assertion.

### 15. Turbofish-Free Value-Based DSL (`rurqe::postgres::prelude`)

Schema markers are zero-sized values, so tables are passed as arguments instead of generic parameters, and the dialect preludes fix the dialect once. A single glob import makes application queries free of `Postgres` annotations and turbofish:

```rust
use rurqe::postgres::prelude::*;

table!(
    /// The `users` table.
    Users => "users" {
        UsersId => "id": i64,
        UsersName => "name": String,
    }
);

table!(
    /// The `orders` table.
    Orders => "orders" {
        OrdersUserId => "user_id": i64,
        OrdersTotal => "total": f64,
    }
);

let built = select_from(Users)
    .inner_join_table(Orders, OrdersUserId.eq(Expr::column::<UsersId>()))
    .select(cols!(UsersId, UsersName, OrdersTotal))
    .where_(UsersId.gt(10i64))
    .order_by_asc(UsersId)
    .limit(20)
    .build();

// SELECT "users"."id", "users"."name", "orders"."total" FROM "users"
//   INNER JOIN "orders" ON ("user_id" = "id") WHERE ("id" > $1) ORDER BY "id" ASC LIMIT 20
```

Projections are checked against the scope built so far, so every join is introduced before `.select(...)`; columns of a `left_join_table(...)` relation still lift into `Option<T>` automatically.

DML entry points take the table value as well, and keep their compile-time guards (`update` / `delete_from` still require `.where_(...)` or `.allow_all()`):

```rust
let inserted = insert_into(Users)
    .values((UsersId::set(1i64), UsersName::set("root")))
    .build();

let updated = update(Users)
    .set(UsersName::set("root"))
    .where_(UsersId.eq(1i64))
    .build()
    .expect("valid query");

let deleted = delete_from(Users)
    .where_(UsersId.eq(1i64))
    .returning((UsersName,))
    .build()
    .expect("valid query");
```

- `rurqe::postgres::prelude::*` re-exports the whole facade prelude and replaces its dialect-generic entry points with PostgreSQL ones, so the dialect is `Postgres<Pg16>` unless a type annotation says otherwise.
- `rurqe::sqlite::prelude::*` provides the identical SQLite entry points (`Sqlite<Sqlite3_35>`).
- Every dialect prelude also re-exports its `.from(table)` extension trait, so `select!(...).from(table)` starts a query without any dialect parameters (see §16).
- The dialect-generic constructors stay available for driver-agnostic code: `select_from::<D, T>()`, `SelectQuery::from_table(table)`, `SelectQuery::inner_join_table(table, on)`, `SelectQuery::left_join_table(table, on)`, `InsertQuery::into_table(table)`, `UpdateQuery::table(table)`, and `DeleteQuery::from_table(table)`.

### 16. Named Selections Without Turbofish & Version-Pinned Preludes

The `select!` macro starts a query straight from a table value through `.from(table)`. Inside a dialect prelude scope this pins the dialect automatically, so neither the dialect nor the row type is written out:

```rust
use rurqe::postgres::prelude::*;

let users = select!(UsersId, UsersName as contact_email)
    .from(Users)
    .where_(UsersId.gt(10i64))
    .order_by_asc(UsersId)
    .build();

// SELECT "users"."id", "users"."name" FROM "users" WHERE ("id" > $1) ORDER BY "id" ASC
```

Version-pinned preludes bind a concrete engine version for the whole entry surface (`select_from`, `insert_into`, `update`, `delete_from`, and `select!(...).from(...)`), so the pinned version's capability gates are checked at compile time:

```rust
use rurqe::postgres::pg14::prelude::*;      // Postgres<Pg14>
use rurqe::postgres::pg15::prelude::*;      // Postgres<Pg15>
use rurqe::postgres::pg16::prelude::*;      // Postgres<Pg16>

use rurqe::sqlite::sqlite3_0::prelude::*;   // Sqlite<Sqlite3_0>
use rurqe::sqlite::sqlite3_24::prelude::*;  // Sqlite<Sqlite3_24>
use rurqe::sqlite::sqlite3_35::prelude::*;  // Sqlite<Sqlite3_35>
```

With a pinned version a capability-gated builder method exists only when that version satisfies the corresponding marker trait:

```rust
use rurqe::sqlite::sqlite3_35::prelude::*;

// `RETURNING` is reachable because SQLite 3.35 implements `SupportsReturning`.
let inserted = insert_into(Users)
    .values((UsersId::set(7i64), UsersName::set("root")))
    .returning(cols!(UsersId, UsersName))
    .build();
```

```rust
use rurqe::sqlite::sqlite3_24::prelude::*;

// `ON CONFLICT` is reachable because SQLite 3.24 implements `SupportsOnConflict`.
let upsert = insert_into(Users)
    .values((UsersId::set(1i64), UsersName::set("root")))
    .on_conflict((UsersId,))
    .do_nothing()
    .build();
```

- Pinning a version turns a version-dependent runtime SQL error into a compile error at the call site.
- The dialect-generic constructors (`select_from::<D, T>()`, `from_table::<D, T>(table)`, `SelectQuery::from_table(table)`, ...) stay available for dialect-agnostic libraries that must not commit to a pinned version.

---

## Pre-flight Build Validation (`BuildError`)

Rendering a statement is fallible. `SelectQuery::build`, `UpdateQuery::build`, and `DeleteQuery::build` return `Result<BuiltQuery, BuildError>`, and every execution helper that renders through them (`fetch_all`, `fetch_optional`, `fetch_one`, `execute`) surfaces the same failure as `ExecutionError::Build`, reachable through `is_build()` and `as_build()` without touching the backend error.

- `BuildError::DuplicateRelation { name }` — two relations share one effective name in `FROM` / `JOIN`, or in the `FROM` / `USING` list of an `UPDATE` / `DELETE` next to the mutated table. The effective name is the alias a relation is referenced under, or its table name when it carries none, so `FROM "users" JOIN "users"` collides exactly like two uses of one alias, and `update(Users).from::<Users>()` collides with the mutated table itself. Give each occurrence a distinct alias via `table_alias!` or `.as_alias(...)`.

Before any SQL leaves the process, the renderer audits the assembled statement tree — the statement itself, its CTEs, its derived tables, its lateral joins, its set-operation operands, and every nested `IN` / `EXISTS` / `MULTISET` / scalar subquery — so a violation in a nested statement is reported through the same typed error as the outermost clause:

- `BuildError::DuplicateRelation { name }` — two relations share one effective name in `FROM` / `JOIN`. The effective name is the alias a relation is referenced under, or its table name when it carries none, so `FROM "users" JOIN "users"` collides exactly like two uses of one alias. Give each occurrence a distinct alias via `table_alias!` or `.as_alias(...)`.
- `BuildError::DistinctOnOrderMismatch { position }` — the leading `ORDER BY` expressions do not match the `DISTINCT ON (...)` expressions left-to-right, which PostgreSQL requires because that ordering decides which duplicate row survives.
- `BuildError::CompoundOrderIndex { index, columns }` — the `ORDER BY` of a compound statement names a 1-based position outside its projection list.
- `BuildError::CompoundOrderColumn { column }` — the `ORDER BY` of a compound statement names an output column its projection list does not produce.

The split follows `Vision.md § 1.5.1`: arity, types, scope, nullability, typestates, and capability gates are compile-time guarantees, while these rules need either a negative assertion (a relation is *absent* from the scope) or the alignment of one clause with another one written later in the chain, so they are decided deterministically by the fallible build.

```rust
use rurqe::prelude::*;

// Rejected while building: the same table appears twice under one name.
let err = select_from::<Postgres<Pg16>, User>()
    .inner_join_table(User, UserId.eq(UserId))
    .select(cols!(UserId))
    .build()
    .unwrap_err();
assert!(matches!(err, BuildError::DuplicateRelation { name: "users" }));

// Guaranteed valid instead: alias the second occurrence.
let alias = TableAlias::new("u2"); // `table_alias!` / `.as_alias(...)` in application code
```

## Domain Newtypes (`#[derive(SqlType)]`)

`#[derive(SqlType)]` gives a domain newtype the same parameter-binding and row-decoding surface as a built-in scalar, so no conversion code is written by hand. Three storage modes cover the common encodings:

- `#[sql(transparent)]` delegates to the wrapped value, so `struct UserId(i64)` binds and decodes exactly like `i64`.
- `#[sql(as = Bytes)]` encodes through `AsRef<[u8]>` and decodes through `TryFrom<&[u8]>`; the optional `len = N` validates that every decoded blob has exactly `N` bytes.
- `#[sql(as = Text)]` encodes through `Display` and decodes through `FromStr`, reporting invalid textual representations as `RowDecodeError::InvalidValue`.

```rust
use rurqe::prelude::*;

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, SqlType)]
#[sql(transparent)]
struct UserId(i64);

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, SqlType)]
#[sql(as = Bytes, len = 4)]
struct Txid([u8; 4]);

#[derive(Debug, PartialEq, Eq, SqlType)]
#[sql(as = Text)]
struct Address(String);
```

Every mode emits `ToSqlVal`, `From<Self> for SqlVal`, `FromSqlValue`, and the expression-compatibility impls, so a derived newtype composes with the expression builders — including `like` / `in_list` for text newtypes — exactly like a built-in scalar. A malformed attribute (`transparent` combined with `as`, `len` without `as = Bytes`, an unknown storage name) is rejected at compile time with an actionable message.

---

## Execution Backends & Runtimes

All execution backends implement `QueryBackend` and `QueryBackendExt`:
- `fetch_all(&mut backend)` -> `Result<Vec<Row>, ExecutionError>`
- `fetch_one(&mut backend)` -> `Result<Row, ExecutionError>` (errors if 0 or >1 rows)
- `fetch_optional(&mut backend)` -> `Result<Option<Row>, ExecutionError>` (errors if >1 rows)
- `execute(&mut backend)` -> `Result<u64, ExecutionError>` (returns affected rows count)

### Typed Errors & `Result<T>` Aliases

Failures are never erased into `Box<dyn std::error::Error>`: every dialect module exports a concrete, monomorphic error type together with a matching alias, so application helpers name the failure once and keep exhaustive pattern matching with zero allocation on the error path.

- `rurqe::postgres::Error` is `ExecutionError<PgError>` and `rurqe::postgres::Result<T, E = Error>` defaults to it.
- `rurqe::sqlite::Error` is `ExecutionError<rusqlite::Error>` and `rurqe::sqlite::Result<T, E = Error>` defaults to it.
- The version-pinned modules (`rurqe::postgres::pg16`, `rurqe::sqlite::sqlite3_35`, ...) define the same aliases, and every dialect prelude re-exports them, so a single glob import is enough.

`ExecutionError<E>` distinguishes four failure kinds, so a caller never has to guess why a statement failed:

```rust
pub enum ExecutionError<E> {
    Backend(E),   // the driver rejected the statement or the connection failed
    RowDecode,    // a returned row did not decode into the projected type
    NoRows,       // `fetch_one` matched nothing
    MultipleRows, // `fetch_one` / `fetch_optional` matched more than one row
}
```

Predicates and accessors keep call sites free of manual enum matching:

- `is_not_found()` -> `bool` — the statement matched no row (`NoRows`).
- `is_multiple_rows()` -> `bool` — `fetch_one` / `fetch_optional` matched several rows.
- `is_row_decode()` -> `bool` — a row carried an unexpected shape or variant.
- `as_backend()` -> `Option<&E>` and `into_backend()` -> `Option<E>` — the driver error stays reachable without downcasting.
- `From<E>` — `?` lifts a concrete driver error into `ExecutionError<E>` automatically.

```rust
use rurqe::prelude::*;
use rurqe::sqlite::{rusqlite::Connection, Sqlite, Sqlite3_35, SqliteConnection};

// The helper names the concrete error type instead of boxing it away.
fn user_name(db: &mut SqliteConnection, id: i64) -> rurqe::sqlite::Result<String> {
    let query = select_from::<Sqlite<Sqlite3_35>, User>()
        .select((UserName,))
        .where_(Expr::column::<UserId>().eq(id));
    let (name,) = db.fetch_one(&query)?;
    Ok(name)
}

let mut db = SqliteConnection::new(Connection::open("app.db")?);

match user_name(&mut db, 42) {
    Ok(name) => println!("found: {name}"),
    Err(error) if error.is_not_found() => println!("no such user"),
    Err(error) => match error.as_backend() {
        Some(driver) => eprintln!("driver failure: {driver}"),
        None => eprintln!("query failure: {error}"),
    },
}
```

### SQLite (Synchronous)

```rust
use rurqe::sqlite::{rusqlite::Connection, Sqlite, Sqlite3_35, SqliteConnection};

let conn = Connection::open("app.db")?;
let mut db = SqliteConnection::new(conn);

let rows = select_from::<Sqlite<Sqlite3_35>, User>()
    .select((UserId, UserName))
    .fetch_all(&mut db)?;
```

### PostgreSQL (Synchronous)

```rust
use rurqe::postgres::{Pg16, PgConnection, Postgres};

let client = postgres::Client::connect("host=localhost user=postgres", postgres::NoTls)?;
let mut db = PgConnection::new(client);

let rows = select_from::<Postgres<Pg16>, User>()
    .select((UserId, UserName))
    .fetch_all(&mut db)?;
```

### PostgreSQL (Asynchronous with Tokio)

```rust
use rurqe::postgres::{Pg16, PgAsyncConnection, Postgres};

let (client, connection) =
    tokio_postgres::connect("host=localhost user=postgres", tokio_postgres::NoTls).await?;
tokio::spawn(async move {
    if let Err(e) = connection.await {
        eprintln!("connection error: {}", e);
    }
});

let db = PgAsyncConnection::new(client);
let rows = db.fetch_all(&select_from::<Postgres<Pg16>, User>().select((UserId, UserName))).await?;
```

---

## RAII Transactions & Savepoints

Transactions enforce panic safety and automatic rollback upon error or panic. Nested transactions are demoted to SQL `SAVEPOINT`s:

### Synchronous Transactions (SQLite & PostgreSQL)

```rust
// SQLite RAII transaction:
let res = db.transaction(|tx| {
    insert_into::<Sqlite, User>()
        .values((UserName::set("alice"), UserActive::set(true)))
        .execute(tx)?;

    // Nested transaction uses SAVEPOINT sp_0:
    tx.transaction(|nested_tx| {
        update::<Sqlite, User>()
            .set(UserName::set("alice_modified"))
            .allow_all()
            .execute(nested_tx)?;
        // Return Err to roll back only the savepoint:
        Err(rurqe::sqlite::rusqlite::Error::ExecuteReturnedResults)
    }).ok();

    // Work outside the rolled-back savepoint is preserved upon Ok:
    Ok(())
})?;

// PostgreSQL synchronous transaction:
pg_db.transaction(|tx| {
    update::<Postgres, User>()
        .set(UserActive::set(true))
        .allow_all()
        .execute(tx)?;
    Ok(())
})?;
```

### Asynchronous Transactions (PostgreSQL)

```rust
let mut tx = db.transaction().await?;

tx.execute(&insert_into::<Postgres, User>().values((UserName::set("async_user"), UserActive::set(true)))).await?;

// Explicit commit (if tx is dropped or future is cancelled, it rolls back automatically):
tx.commit().await?;
```

---

## Connection Pooling

Connection pools directly implement `QueryBackend` with zero boilerplate (no manual `pool.get()` needed):

```rust
// Synchronous r2d2 pool (SQLite & PostgreSQL):
use rurqe::sqlite::SqlitePool;
let manager = r2d2_sqlite::SqliteConnectionManager::file("app.db");
let pool = SqlitePool::new(r2d2::Pool::new(manager)?);

// Queries can be executed directly against &pool:
let users = select_from::<Sqlite, User>()
    .select((UserId, UserName))
    .fetch_all(&pool)?;

// Asynchronous deadpool pool (PostgreSQL):
use rurqe::postgres::PgAsyncPool;
let mut cfg = deadpool_postgres::Config::new();
let pool = PgAsyncPool::new(cfg.create_pool(None, tokio_postgres::NoTls)?);

let users = pool.fetch_all(&select_from::<Postgres, User>().select((UserId, UserName))).await?;
```

---

## Migrations & Schema Lifecycle

Migrations support Flyway conventions (`V` for versioned, `R` for repeatable):

```rust
use rurqe::migrate::Error;
use rurqe::prelude::embed_migrations;

fn main() -> Result<(), Error> {
    // Without an argument the macro starts at `CARGO_MANIFEST_DIR`, walks its
    // ancestors for `rurqe.toml`, and resolves `[migrations].dir` — or
    // `<root>/migrations` when the file declares none.
    let migrations = embed_migrations!()?;

    // One optional argument replaces the walk: a file is a `rurqe.toml`
    // resolved against the manifest directory of the crate being compiled, so
    // the macro never accepts a directory. Only the `*.sql` files of the
    // migration directory itself are baked in, so `checkpoint.toml` and
    // `checkpoint-stage/` stay artifacts of the toolchain.
    let explicit = embed_migrations!("db/rurqe.toml")?;

    println!(
        "{} and {} embedded migration(s)",
        migrations.len(),
        explicit.len()
    );
    Ok(())
}
```

---

## Stage + Migration Tail Lifecycle

A project may describe its schema twice instead of replaying the whole history: the declarative stage (`schema/`) and the active migration tail (`migrations/`). Both descriptions must converge on exactly the same state — the golden equation `State(schema/) == State(Checkpoint + migrations/)`.

```text
project/
├── rurqe.toml                    # Schemas, artifact layout, codegen settings
└── rurqe/                        # Artifact directory (`root`, default `rurqe`)
    ├── schema/                   # Declarative target DDL (single source of truth)
    │   ├── users.sql
    │   └── orders.sql
    ├── migrations/               # Active tail above the checkpoint boundary
    │   ├── V051__add_credits.sql # DDL + DML delta
    │   ├── V052__index_billing.sql
    │   ├── checkpoint.toml       # pruned_up_to_version + schema_hash of the base stage
    │   └── checkpoint-stage/     # Verbatim DDL snapshot of the checkpoint boundary
    └── schema.lock               # Versioned TOML v5 catalog snapshot (SCHEMA_HASH)
```

The `schema.lock` snapshot is the versioned TOML v5 document (`version = 5`): the writer serializes the engine-neutral `SchemaCatalog` through strongly typed `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]` DTOs, and enums, tables, views, and triggers — as well as each table's columns, checks, foreign keys, and indexes — are sorted by name while every entity carries the schema it belongs to, so the snapshot and its `SCHEMA_HASH` depend only on the schema content. Snapshots of the legacy v1–v3 text formats and of the previous v4 TOML document remain readable; a project upgrading from a pre-v4 snapshot re-runs `cargo rurqe codegen` (or `cargo rurqe stage commit`) once, because the snapshot bytes — and with them `SCHEMA_HASH` and the checkpoint hashes — change with the format.

Absent `rurqe/schema/` and `rurqe/migrations/checkpoint.toml`, the runner keeps the classic sequential Flyway behaviour with no configuration at all.

### Cold Start from the Declarative Stage

```rust
use rurqe::migrate::{
    cold_start, DeclarativeStage, SchemaCatalog, StageMarker, StageScript,
};

let stage = DeclarativeStage::new(vec![
    StageScript::new("orders.sql", "CREATE TABLE orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY);"),
    StageScript::new(
        "users.sql",
        "CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, email TEXT NOT NULL);",
    ),
]);
let marker = StageMarker::from_catalog("3.2".parse().expect("a valid version"), &SchemaCatalog::default());

let report = cold_start(&mut backend, &stage, &marker)?;
```

- `DeclarativeStage::load(Path::new("rurqe/schema"))` reads every `*.sql` file in name order, so the applied DDL is deterministic; a missing directory is reported as `Ok(None)`.
- Every script runs inside one transaction and a synthetic `<< Stage >>` baseline marker is recorded, so migrations at or below the marker version are already applied while the tail above it still runs.
- Repeating the same stage (same version and digest) is a no-op; a diverged digest or an already initialised database fails with `Error::BaselineAlreadyExists` instead of overwriting the schema.

### Checkpoints and Zero-Pain Pruning

```rust
use rurqe::migrate::{Checkpoint, Checksum, Migrator};

let checkpoint = Checkpoint::new("4".parse().expect("a valid version"), Checksum::of(b"..."));
let report = Migrator::with_checkpoint(checkpoint).migrate(&mut backend, &tail)?;
```

- `Checkpoint::parse` / `Checkpoint::load` read the `[checkpoint]` table (`pruned_up_to_version`, `schema_hash`), while `Checkpoint::render` writes it back canonically.
- `Checkpoint::validate_history` compares the newest recorded version with the boundary: a target at or above it is advanced by the tail, while a target below it — or one that recorded no version at all — fails with `Error::OutdatedCheckpoint` carrying an actionable remedy instead of a partial replay.
- Because the marker anchors the base stage, migration files below the boundary can be deleted freely (`rm -f rurqe/migrations/V001...V050*.sql`) without rewriting baselines or invalidating checksums.

### Golden Equation Verification

`rurqe_cli::stage::GoldenEquation` materialises both sides in a disposable scratch state — an in-memory SQLite database, or a PostgreSQL transaction that is always rolled back — introspects the resulting catalogs, and compares them structurally:

```rust
use rurqe_cli::stage::GoldenEquation;

let report = GoldenEquation::new(&stage, &tail)
    .with_base(&base_stage) // the stage snapshot the checkpoint was cut at
    .with_schema("app") // the PostgreSQL schema both sides are read over (`public` by default)
    .verify(":memory:")?;

assert!(report.is_equivalent());
assert_eq!(report.stage_hash(), report.tail_hash());
```

`GoldenEquation::with_schema` selects the PostgreSQL schema both sides are materialised into and introspected over, defaulting to `public`; a SQLite scratch holds a single unnamed catalog and ignores the name. `cargo rurqe stage verify --schema <name>` applies the same selection through the shared precedence (`--schema` > the `schema` key of `rurqe.toml` > `public`), so a project keeping its relations outside `public` compares the catalogs it really declares. A scratch materialisation whose selection describes nothing while the server keeps user relations elsewhere is reported in the command's output instead of certifying an empty comparison.

A divergence is returned as `StageError::Diverged` carrying the full report — missing or extra tables and columns, altered column definitions, and primary/foreign key mismatches — so CI fails with the exact gap instead of a production incident.

The boundary the checkpoint anchors is recorded by the toolchain itself: `stage commit` snapshots the declarative stage verbatim into a `checkpoint-stage/` directory next to `checkpoint.toml`, and `stage verify` always loads that snapshot as the base stage. A checkpoint whose non-empty boundary has no base stage to replay is rejected with `StageError::BaseStageMissing` before any scratch database is opened, instead of replaying the filtered tail over an empty database and reporting a consistent project as diverged. An empty boundary is the one exception: an empty scratch database reproduces it on its own.

---

## Toolchain CLI Commands

The `rurqe-cli` toolchain manages database lifecycles for both PostgreSQL and SQLite, and it carries no engine protocol of its own: the backends and the catalog introspection it drives are the ones the driver crates ship, so a command and a binary applying its own embedded collection run the same protocol.

Every command resolves its artifacts the same way: `--config <PATH>` names the project configuration, the conventional `rurqe.toml` of the working directory applies when the flag names none, and every path — the migration tail, the declarative stage, the boundary marker, the catalog snapshot, the generated module — comes from that file or from the conventional layout beneath its artifact directory. No command accepts a flag of its own for an individual path.

- `cargo rurqe migrate up [--database-url <URL>] [--schema <NAME>] [--config <PATH>]` — Apply pending versioned and modified repeatable migrations; the boundary marker the project configuration resolves arms the guard that refuses a target older than the pruned boundary.
- `cargo rurqe migrate status [--database-url <URL>] [--schema <NAME>] [--config <PATH>]` — Inspect migration statuses against `__rurqe_schema_history`.
- `cargo rurqe migrate repair [--database-url <URL>] [--schema <NAME>] [--config <PATH>]` — Realign checksums and purge failed attempts.
- `cargo rurqe baseline --version <V> [--description <DESC>] [--database-url <URL>] [--config <PATH>]` — Baseline pre-existing schemas without historical replay.
- `cargo rurqe codegen [--domain-types] [--schema <NAME>] [--database-url <URL>] [--config <PATH>]` — Introspect the live database (`postgres://...`, `postgresql://...`, `sqlite://...`, or a local file), generate the Rust schema, and write the catalog snapshot (`rurqe/schema.lock` beneath the artifact directory). The module goes to `[codegen].output` of `rurqe.toml`, otherwise to `src/schema.rs`. Schema names are sanitized into valid Rust identifiers (`2fa` → `_2fa`, `user.email` → `user_email`), Rust keywords are escaped (`type` → `r#type`, `self` → `self_`), and two names that reduce to the same identifier fail codegen with an error listing the conflicting names instead of emitting duplicate definitions. `Uuid`, `Json`, `Timestamp`, `Date`, and engine-specific columns are generated as `String` unless `[codegen].domain_types` or `--domain-types` maps them onto the ecosystem types. The optional `[codegen.type_overrides]` table maps a `table.column` (or `schema.table.column`) path onto the Rust type generated for that column, so domain newtypes survive code generation: `"users.id" = "uuid::Uuid"`, `users.created_at = "chrono::NaiveDateTime"`, and `"wallets.address" = "bitcoin::Address"` next to `"transactions.txid" = "bitcoin::Txid"`; the declared nullability still applies, wrapping a nullable override into `Option<T>` and never wrapping an already optional type twice.
- `cargo rurqe verify [--schema <NAME>] [--database-url <URL>] [--config <PATH>]` — CI drift verification: verifies bit-for-bit parity between the live database catalog, the catalog snapshot (`rurqe/schema.lock` beneath the artifact directory), and the embedded `pub const SCHEMA_HASH` of the module `[codegen].output` names — the conventional `src/schema.rs` when that key names none, and the snapshot alone when neither exists.
- `cargo rurqe stage init --version <V> [--description <DESC>] [--schema <NAME>] [--database-url <URL>] [--config <PATH>]` — Cold start an empty database from the declarative stage (`rurqe/schema` beneath the artifact directory) in one transaction and record the synthetic `<< Stage >>` baseline marker.
- `cargo rurqe stage verify [--scratch-url <URL>] [--database-url <URL>] [--schema <NAME>] [--config <PATH>]` — Verify the golden equation `State(schema/) == State(Checkpoint + migrations/)` in a disposable scratch database; the boundary snapshot recorded by `stage commit` is always the base stage, and divergence is reported per table and column.
- `cargo rurqe stage commit --version <V> [--schema <NAME>] [--database-url <URL>] [--config <PATH>]` — Introspect the live database, write the catalog snapshot (`rurqe/schema.lock` beneath the artifact directory), snapshot the boundary stage verbatim into `<stem>-stage/` next to the marker — `checkpoint-stage/` beside `checkpoint.toml` — and anchor the marker; the parity gate refuses a stage that does not describe the database, and the boundary can never be rewound to an older version.
- `cargo rurqe stage cleanup [--scratch-url <URL>] [--database-url <URL>] [--older-than <SECS>] [--yes|--force] [--config <PATH>]` — Drop the PostgreSQL scratch databases abandoned by earlier verifications.
- `cargo rurqe prune --before <V> [--dry-run] [--config <PATH>]` — Delete migration scripts below the committed checkpoint boundary; the command refuses to drop anything above it, because the active tail still needs those scripts.

An application never needs the command line for either route. The facade enables the `migrate` feature of the drivers a build includes, so a collection baked by `embed_migrations!` applies over a backend that borrows the connection the application already holds, and `migrate_async` runs the same protocol on a dedicated blocking thread and hands the backend back to the caller.
